approachQuestion.prompt: Concurrent job peak — Find the largest number of jobs active at the same time and the earliest time when that peak occurs. A job is active during the half-open interval [start, end): it is active at start and inactive at end. If there are no jobs, return (0, null). Example: [[1,4), [4,8)] returns (1, 1), because the first job is no longer active at time 4. Example: [[1,4), [4,8), [2,6), [6,9), [3,5)] returns (3, 3).
constraints: The input is an unsorted list of n jobs; 0 ≤ n ≤ 200,000.
Each job has integer times 0 ≤ start < end ≤ 1,000,000,000. Duplicate intervals represent different jobs.
Return a pair (maximum number of active jobs, earliest start time at which that number is reached). For empty input, the time is null. Do not modify the input.

options.text: Create a start event (+1) and an end event (−1) for each job. Sort the events by time, processing ends before starts when times tie. Count active jobs, and after processing starts update the maximum and its earliest time.
options.feedback: For [start,end), a job is not active at end, so jobs ending at a time must be removed before jobs starting at that same time are added. The sorted events visit every time when the peak can be reached.

options.text: Create separate lists of start times and end times, sort both lists, then scan through the times in ascending order. Subtract ends before adding starts when times tie. After adding starts, check the maximum and its earliest time.
options.feedback: This is an equivalent scan over the ordered starts and ends. The tie order preserves the half-open interval rule, and a later tie does not replace the earlier time.

options.text: For each distinct start time, count from the beginning how many intervals satisfy start ≤ that time < end. Return the largest count and the earliest start time with that count.
options.feedback: This method finds the correct maximum for every valid input because a peak occurs when some job starts. However, it scans all jobs again for each start instead of ordering the events and scanning them once; this is brute force, not a near-optimal method.

options.text: Sort events by time, but when times tie, add jobs that start before removing jobs that end.
options.feedback: This counts two jobs at the same time even though the first one has already ended. For [1,4) and [4,8), it reports a maximum of 2 instead of 1.

feedback.reason: Consider separately whether the method follows the exact endpoint rules and whether it does only the necessary work.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed `sorted-endpoint-events` method, choose the time and auxiliary-space pair. Do not count the input or returned pair; the array of 2n events is auxiliary space.
constraints: Analyze only the specified method. The input is already in memory and is not auxiliary space. The returned output is excluded from auxiliary space.
Each comparison, addition, assignment, and numeric-key comparison takes O(1); arithmetic does not overflow.

options.text: Time O(n log n), auxiliary space O(n)
Time O(n log n), auxiliary space O(1)

feedback.reason: The method creates exactly 2n events and sorts them; the later scan is linear. The event list uses linear space. The earliest peak time needs only a fixed number of variables.

details.assumptions: Comparison-based sorting of 2n events. Stability is not needed because the tie-break order is explicit: end before start. For n=0, return (0,null).

methodReveal.title: Count events along the timeline
methodReveal.description: Turn each job into two events: a start increases the count, and an end decreases it. Order events by time. At the same time, process ends before starts because an interval stops at its end while another begins at its start. After processing starts, check the count and keep the first time that reaches a new peak.
